hook: At forty-one thousand feet, both engines of this brand new jet went silent.

blocks.narration: At forty-one thousand feet, both engines of this brand new jet went silent. The fuel tanks were completely empty.
blocks.visual: A jet's engines stop high above the clouds

shots.visual: Pearson in a dim airliner cockpit, his face lit red by flashing warning lights, eyes wide in shock, hands on the control yoke
beats: red warning lights flash across his face
he grips the yoke hard
the glowing screens in front of him snap to black

shots.visual: The Jet high above golden sunset clouds, thin smoke trailing from both engines
beats: the smoke trails from both engines thin out
the jet glides on in silence, nose dipping slightly

shots.visual: Cross-section cutaway of the Jet's wing showing its fuel tank completely dry, one last drop of fuel at the bottom

blocks.narration: The fuel gauge was broken, so the crew did the math by hand. But this jet measured fuel in kilograms, not pounds.
blocks.visual: The crew works out fuel by hand

shots.visual: Pearson and Quintal standing under the Jet's wing, Quintal writing on a clipboard while Pearson watches
beats: Quintal scribbles fast on the clipboard
Pearson leans in and taps the page
they both nod, satisfied

shots.visual: Quintal's pencil over the clipboard, the Jet's wing and the Fuel truck behind him
beats: Quintal writes a number
he pauses, then underlines it with a confident stroke

blocks.narration: Mixing them up, the crew loaded less than half the fuel they needed. Halfway to Edmonton, the jet ran dry.
blocks.visual: Too little fuel, then the engines stop

shots.visual: The Fuel truck parked under the Jet's wing, its thick hose running up into the wing
beats: the hose shudders as fuel pumps
the pump stops early
the hose goes slack

shots.visual: Quintal in the cockpit, tapping a cockpit screen as its glow flickers
beats: the screen flickers
Quintal taps it twice
it goes dark and his jaw drops

blocks.narration: Luckily, Captain Bob Pearson was also a glider pilot. He flew the silent jet for seventeen minutes, looking for a runway.

shots.visual: Pearson at the controls, calm and focused, the yoke in both hands, sunset light through the cockpit window
beats: Pearson takes a slow breath
he eases the yoke forward
he gives a small, determined nod

shots.visual: The Jet gliding low and silent over green fields and blue lakes at sunset, its shadow sliding across the fields
beats: the jet glides forward over a lake
its shadow slides across the fields

blocks.narration: His co-pilot knew an old air base at Gimli, now a racetrack. All sixty-nine survived, and the jet got a nickname: the Gimli Glider.
blocks.visual: The jet lands on a racetrack; everyone survives

shots.visual: The Jet descending toward the Gimli strip, race cars with dark tinted windows parked along the far end
beats: the jet sinks lower over the strip
its wheels touch the runway with a puff of smoke

shots.visual: Pearson smiling beside the nose of the Jet resting on the Gimli strip, passengers sliding down an orange evacuation slide behind him
beats: passengers slide down the slide, cheering
Pearson pats the jet's nose
he grins and gives a big thumbs-up

captions.hook_line: A brand new jet ran out of fuel at 41,000 feet because of a pounds-and-kilograms mix-up ✈️
captions.body: On July 23, 1983, Air Canada Flight 143 left with 22,300 pounds of fuel instead of the 22,300 kilograms it needed, less than half the right load. Captain Bob Pearson, an experienced glider pilot, glided the Boeing 767 for 17 minutes to Gimli, Manitoba. All 69 aboard survived, and the plane flew until 2008.
captions.comment_prompt: Would you have trusted the gauge or the math?

youtube_title: This Jet Ran Out of Fuel at 41,000 Feet

sources.claim: Fuel load 22,300 lb instead of 22,300 kg, less than half needed; FQIS broken; first Air Canada jets calibrated in metric; ran out halfway to Edmonton at 41,000 ft; glided 17 minutes; Pearson an experienced sailplane pilot; Gimli converted to a racetrack; 69 aboard, no serious injuries; nickname Gimli Glider; in service until 2008
